planMarkdown:
Bot: Production-ready Telegram crypto price and alerts bot

Summary:
A single-process Node.js ESM Telegram bot built with grammY that lets users manage crypto watchlists, look up live prices, create above and below price alerts, and receive notifications when targets are hit.

The bot uses a provider abstraction over CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap so price data can be fetched consistently, cached safely, and degraded gracefully when one provider is unavailable. MongoDB is used for durable user, watchlist, alert, and notification state, while in-memory caching protects external APIs from excessive calls and improves response speed.

The design prioritizes simple Telegram UX, reliable alert delivery, predictable error handling, and operational safety within the constraint of one Node.js service/process.

Product goals:
The bot should provide a fast and simple Telegram interface for everyday crypto tracking.

1) Users can look up a coin price with a command such as /price btc and receive current price, 24h percentage change, provider timestamp, and quick actions.

2) Users can build a personal watchlist by adding and removing coin symbols, then view the watchlist with current prices and 24h changes.

3) Users can create price alerts for specific coins using above or below conditions. Alerts should be easy to list, remove, pause, or recreate.

4) The bot should notify users when alert targets are reached and avoid repeated spam for the same trigger.

5) The bot should handle provider downtime, invalid symbols, rate limits, and slow responses gracefully. When live data is unavailable, it should use cached data where safe and clearly tell users when data may be stale.

6) The UX should use Telegram inline buttons for common actions such as add to watchlist, remove from watchlist, add alert, list alerts, and refresh price.

7) The system should be production-ready but intentionally simple: one Node.js process, grammY for Telegram, MongoDB for persistence, in-memory caches for runtime optimization, and no additional queues or infrastructure.

High-level architecture:
The bot runs as a single Node.js ESM service using grammY. It starts with TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN from environment variables, initializes MongoDB, loads bot commands, registers command and callback handlers, and starts an in-process alert scheduler.

Core components:

1) Telegram interface layer
Handles grammY commands, callback queries, message parsing, inline keyboards, and response formatting. This layer should stay thin and delegate business logic to services.

2) User service
Creates or updates user records when a user interacts with the bot. Stores Telegram user id, username, locale, preferences, and status.

3) Coin resolution service
Normalizes user input such as btc, BTC, bitcoin, eth, or ethereum into a canonical coin identity. This is important because symbols are ambiguous. The service should prefer known high-liquidity mappings and store provider-specific ids.

4) Price provider layer
Defines a common internal interface for fetching prices, 24h change, market metadata, and symbol search. Implement adapters for CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap. One provider can be primary and the other fallback. Responses should be normalized into one internal format.

5) Cache layer
Uses in-memory maps with TTLs for recent prices, coin search results, provider health, and negative lookups. This reduces API usage, improves latency, and protects the bot from rate limits. MongoDB can optionally store longer-lived coin metadata and last known prices, but hot cache should remain in memory.

6) Watchlist service
Manages user watchlist items in MongoDB. It validates coin symbols through the coin resolution service and avoids duplicates.

7) Alert service
Manages alert creation, listing, removal, state transitions, and trigger evaluation. Alerts are persisted in MongoDB so they survive process restarts.

8) Notification service
Sends Telegram messages when alerts trigger. It records notification attempts and results to support idempotency and debugging.

9) Alert scheduler
Runs inside the same Node.js process on a fixed interval. It loads active alerts, groups them by coin, fetches prices efficiently in batches when possible, evaluates thresholds, and dispatches notifications. It should use a simple in-process lock flag to prevent overlapping scheduler ticks.

10) Error handling and fallback layer
Centralizes user-safe errors. Provider errors should not leak raw stack traces. If live data fails but cached data exists, the bot should respond with a stale-data notice. If no data is available, it should show a clear API down message and suggest retrying later.

The recommended runtime flow is request driven for commands and interval driven for alert checks. Because the service is a single process, all background tasks must be lightweight, bounded, and defensive against slow APIs.

Data model:
Use MongoDB for durable persistence. In-memory maps are used for short-lived runtime caching only.

Suggested collections:

1) users
Fields: telegramUserId, chatId, username, firstName, languageCode, timezone, currencyPreference, isBlocked, createdAt, updatedAt, lastSeenAt.

Purpose: identify where to send notifications, store user preferences, and track whether messages can still be delivered.

2) coins
Fields: coinId, symbol, name, aliases, providerIds, rank, isActive, lastResolvedAt, createdAt, updatedAt.

Purpose: cache canonical coin metadata and reduce repeated provider search calls. providerIds can include the CoinGecko id and CoinMarketCap id when available.

3) watchlistItems
Fields: userId, coinId, symbol, name, createdAt.

Recommended indexes: unique combination of userId and coinId.

Purpose: store each user’s watchlist without duplicates.

4) alerts
Fields: userId, chatId, coinId, symbol, name, direction, targetPrice, currency, status, triggerOnce, cooldownMinutes, lastCheckedPrice, lastCheckedAt, triggeredAt, lastNotifiedAt, createdAt, updatedAt.

Valid direction values: above, below.

Valid status values: active, triggered, paused, deleted.

Purpose: store active and historical price alerts. For a simple UX, alerts should default to triggerOnce true, meaning they become triggered after notification. A future setting can support recurring alerts with cooldown.

5) notificationLogs
Fields: userId, chatId, alertId, coinId, type, message, status, telegramMessageId, errorCode, errorMessage, createdAt.

Purpose: record alert notification attempts and prevent duplicate sends during scheduler retries.

6) providerStatus
Fields: providerName, status, lastSuccessAt, lastFailureAt, failureCount, lastError, updatedAt.

Purpose: track provider health and support fallback decisions.

7) optional priceSnapshots
Fields: coinId, currency, price, change24h, providerName, fetchedAt, expiresAt.

Purpose: store last known prices across restarts if desired. This is optional because the main price cache can be in memory, but storing last known values improves API down fallback behavior after a restart.

In-memory caches:

1) priceCache keyed by coinId and currency, with a short TTL such as 30 to 60 seconds.

2) coinSearchCache keyed by normalized user input, with a longer TTL such as several hours.

3) negativeLookupCache keyed by invalid symbol input, with a shorter TTL such as 5 to 15 minutes.

4) providerHealthCache keyed by provider name, used to avoid hammering a failing API.

Data consistency principles:

1) Store canonical coin identity, not only raw symbols.

2) Keep alerts durable before confirming creation to the user.

3) Mark alerts as triggered before or atomically with notification logging where practical to reduce duplicate notifications.

4) Treat external prices as eventually consistent and always include timestamps when data may be cached or stale.

Key flows:
Onboarding flow:

1) User sends /start.

2) Bot creates or updates the user record.

3) Bot replies with a short explanation and inline buttons: Price lookup, Add to watchlist, My watchlist, Create alert, My alerts.

Price lookup flow:

1) User sends /price btc.

2) Bot normalizes btc and resolves it to a canonical coin.

3) Bot checks the in-memory price cache.

4) If cache is fresh, return the cached price immediately.

5) If cache is missing or expired, fetch from the primary provider.

6) If the primary provider fails, fetch from the fallback provider.

7) If both fail but a last known price exists, reply with stale price plus an API down notice.

8) If no usable data exists, reply with a graceful fallback message.

9) Response includes inline buttons such as Add to watchlist, Add alert, Refresh, and View watchlist.

Watchlist add flow:

1) User sends /add btc or taps Add to watchlist from a price result.

2) Bot resolves the coin.

3) Bot creates the watchlist item if it does not already exist.

4) Bot confirms and offers buttons for View watchlist and Add alert.

Watchlist list flow:

1) User sends /watchlist.

2) Bot loads the user’s watchlist.

3) Bot groups coin ids and fetches prices efficiently, using cache where possible.

4) Bot returns a compact list with price and 24h change.

5) Each row or summary includes quick actions where practical: Refresh, Remove, Add alert.

Watchlist remove flow:

1) User sends /remove btc or taps Remove.

2) Bot resolves or matches the coin from the user’s watchlist.

3) Bot deletes the item and confirms.

Alert creation flow:

1) User sends a command such as /alert btc above 70000 or taps Add alert.

2) Bot validates symbol, direction, and target price.

3) Bot fetches current price to provide context.

4) Bot stores an active alert in MongoDB.

5) Bot confirms with current price, target price, direction, and buttons for My alerts and Remove alert.

Alert listing flow:

1) User sends /alerts.

2) Bot lists active alerts first, then recently triggered alerts if useful.

3) Each alert shows coin, direction, target, current or last checked price, and status.

4) Inline buttons allow removing or pausing individual alerts.

Alert removal flow:

1) User sends /removealert alertId or taps a Remove alert button.

2) Bot verifies that the alert belongs to the user.

3) Bot marks the alert deleted rather than hard deleting it.

4) Bot confirms removal.

Notification flow:

1) Scheduler wakes up at a fixed interval such as every 30 to 60 seconds.

2) Scheduler loads active alerts due for checking.

3) Scheduler groups alerts by coin and currency.

4) Scheduler fetches current prices with cache and provider fallback.

5) For each alert, scheduler checks whether the condition is met: above means current price is greater than or equal to target; below means current price is less than or equal to target.

6) If met, scheduler marks trigger state and sends a Telegram notification.

7) Notification includes coin, current price, target price, direction, 24h change, and buttons such as View alerts, Create another alert, and View price.

8) If Telegram reports that the user blocked the bot, mark the user as blocked and stop sending future notifications.

Provider failure flow:

1) On timeout, rate limit, invalid response, or server error, record provider failure.

2) Try fallback provider if available and healthy.

3) If all providers fail, use fresh-enough cached data if available.

4) If only stale data is available, clearly label it as last known price.

5) If no data is available, show: Price API is temporarily unavailable. Please try again later.

Inline button flow:

1) Callback payloads should be compact and contain action plus stable ids, not untrusted full user input.

2) Every callback must verify ownership when modifying user data.

3) Callback handlers should answer callback queries quickly to avoid Telegram loading spinners.

4) For destructive actions, either confirm with a second button or make removal easy to undo where appropriate.

Tech stack:
Runtime and language:

1) Node.js using ESM modules.

2) Single Node.js service/process.

3) Environment variable TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN for the Telegram bot token.

Telegram framework:

1) grammY for Telegram Bot API integration.

2) grammY command handlers for slash commands.

3) grammY callback query handlers for inline buttons.

4) grammY middleware for logging, user upsert, error boundaries, and request context.

Persistence:

1) MongoDB for durable storage of users, watchlists, alerts, provider status, and notification logs.

2) In-memory maps for short-lived price cache, coin lookup cache, and provider health cache.

3) No additional databases, external queues, or separate worker infrastructure.

External price APIs:

1) CoinGecko adapter for price lookup, market data, and symbol resolution.

2) CoinMarketCap adapter as an alternative or fallback provider.

3) Internal normalized price format so the rest of the bot is independent of provider-specific response shapes.

4) Provider timeouts, retry limits, rate limit handling, and circuit-breaker style health tracking implemented inside the single service.

Scheduling:

1) In-process interval scheduler for alert checks.

2) No external message queue.

3) Use a non-overlap guard so a slow alert check does not start another concurrent tick.

Deployment:

1) Run as a Node.js server in the cloud.

2) Use long polling or webhook mode depending on the deployment environment. Long polling is simpler for one service. Webhook mode can be used if the server exposes a stable HTTPS endpoint.

3) Graceful shutdown should stop Telegram polling or webhook handling, stop the alert scheduler, finish in-flight operations briefly, and close MongoDB connections.

Configuration:

1) TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN is required.

2) MongoDB connection string is required when persistence is enabled.

3) CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap configuration should be environment-driven.

4) Cache TTLs, alert check interval, provider timeout, and max watchlist size should be configurable.

Non-functional requirements:
Reliability:

1) All command handlers should catch expected errors and return user-friendly messages.

2) External API calls must have timeouts.

3) Provider fallback should be automatic when the primary provider fails.

4) Cached last known prices should be used for degraded responses when safe.

5) Alert scheduler must prevent overlapping runs.

6) Alert notifications must be idempotent enough to avoid duplicate spam.

Performance:

1) Cache price lookups for a short TTL to reduce provider calls.

2) Batch or group price requests by coin whenever provider APIs allow it.

3) Avoid fetching prices one by one for watchlists and alert checks.

4) Limit watchlist size and number of active alerts per user to protect the single process.

Security and abuse prevention:

1) Validate all command arguments.

2) Never trust callback payloads without checking ownership in MongoDB.

3) Do not expose provider errors, tokens, database details, or stack traces to users.

4) Rate limit high-cost commands per user in memory.

5) Keep secrets in environment variables only.

Observability:

1) Structured logs for command handling, provider calls, alert checks, and notification sends.

2) Track provider failure counts and last successful fetch time.

3) Log slow scheduler ticks and unusually large batches.

4) Store notification logs for debugging alert delivery.

User experience:

1) Keep responses compact and readable on mobile.

2) Always show the interpreted coin name when a user enters a symbol.

3) For ambiguous symbols, ask the user to choose from inline buttons.

4) Include timestamps or freshness hints for cached or stale prices.

5) Use consistent formatting for prices, percentages, and alert states.

Operational limits:

1) Suggested default watchlist limit: 50 coins per user.

2) Suggested default active alert limit: 50 alerts per user.

3) Suggested price cache TTL: 30 to 60 seconds.

4) Suggested alert check interval: 30 to 60 seconds, adjusted according to provider rate limits.

5) Suggested provider request timeout: 5 to 10 seconds.

Graceful degradation:

1) If live APIs are down but cached data exists, reply with last known price and clear stale warning.

2) If a specific symbol cannot be resolved, suggest examples such as BTC, ETH, SOL.

3) If the user has no watchlist or alerts, show an empty-state message with quick action buttons.

4) If the bot cannot send a notification because the user blocked it, mark the user blocked and suppress future sends until they interact again.

Bot commands:
• start — Starts the bot, creates or updates the user profile, and shows the main menu with quick actions. (usage: /start) [general]
• help — Shows available commands, examples, and a short explanation of watchlists and alerts. (usage: /help) [general]
• price — Looks up the current price and 24h change for a coin symbol or name. (usage: /price btc) [prices]
• add — Adds a coin to the user’s watchlist after resolving and validating the symbol. (usage: /add btc) [watchlist]
• remove — Removes a coin from the user’s watchlist. (usage: /remove btc) [watchlist]
• watchlist — Lists the user’s watched coins with current prices and 24h changes. (usage: /watchlist) [watchlist]
• alert — Creates an above or below price alert for a coin. (usage: /alert btc above 70000) [alerts]
• alerts — Lists the user’s active and recently triggered alerts with quick removal actions. (usage: /alerts) [alerts]
• removealert — Removes an alert by id. The id is shown in the alert list and inline buttons can be used instead. (usage: /removealert 12345) [alerts]
• settings — Shows user preferences such as display currency and notification behavior. (usage: /settings) [settings]

Crypto Watcher Bot

Crypto Watcher is a Telegram bot for cryptocurrency prices, watchlists, and price alerts. It uses CoinGecko first, then CoinMarketCap only when COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY is configured. MongoDB stores users, watchlists, alerts, coin metadata, and cached prices.

Commands

/start
Shows the welcome message and inline buttons for Price Lookup, Watchlist, Add Alert, and Help.

/help
Lists commands and examples.

/price <symbol>
Shows current USD price and 24h change.
Example: /price BTC

/watchlist
Shows your saved coins with prices when available.

/addwatch <symbol>
Adds a coin to your watchlist.
Example: /addwatch SOL

/removewatch <symbol>
Removes a coin from your watchlist.
Example: /removewatch ETH

/alert <symbol> <above|below> <price>
Creates a one-time alert.
Examples: /alert BTC above 90000, /alert ETH below 2500

/alerts
Lists your active and recently triggered alerts with IDs.

/removealert <id>
Removes an alert. Use /alerts to find the ID.

Environment variables

TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN is required. It is the Telegram token from BotFather.

MONGODB_URI is required. It stores users, watchlists, alerts, cached coin metadata, cached prices, and notification logs.

COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY is optional. If present, CoinMarketCap is used as a fallback when CoinGecko is unavailable.

ALERT_POLL_MS is optional and defaults to 60000.

MARKET_TIMEOUT_MS is optional and defaults to 10000.

PRICE_CACHE_TTL_MS is optional and defaults to 45000.

SYMBOL_CACHE_TTL_MS is optional and defaults to 21600000.

Setup

1) Copy .env.sample to .env.
2) Set TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and MONGODB_URI.
3) Run npm install.
4) Run npm run dev for local development.
5) Run npm start for production.

Deployment notes

The bot runs as one Node.js process. It uses grammY long polling through @grammyjs/runner. On boot it clears any Telegram webhook with drop_pending_updates to avoid webhook and polling conflicts.

Alert notifications

The in-process polling loop checks active alerts at ALERT_POLL_MS. It groups alerts by coin, fetches prices in batches where possible, marks triggered alerts inactive, and sends one notification per triggered alert.

Troubleshooting

If the bot exits on startup, verify TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and MONGODB_URI are set.

If prices are unavailable, CoinGecko may be rate limited or down. If cached prices exist, the bot labels them as cached or stale. If no cache exists, it asks the user to try later.

If MongoDB fails to connect, check the network allowlist, username, password, and database URI.

Logs never print secrets. Startup logs show only whether each env var is set.

README.md.content:
Crypto Watcher Bot

A production-ready Telegram bot for crypto prices, watchlists, and one-time price alerts.

Features

1) /price BTC returns USD price and 24h change.
2) /watchlist, /addwatch, and /removewatch manage saved coins.
3) /alert, /alerts, and /removealert manage above and below alerts.
4) Inline buttons support refresh, watchlist, add alert, remove, and help actions.
5) CoinGecko is the primary market API.
6) CoinMarketCap is an optional fallback when COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY is present.
7) MongoDB stores users, watchlists, alerts, cached coin metadata, cached prices, and notification logs.
8) The alert polling loop runs in the same Node.js process.

Architecture

src/index.js boots the process, validates env vars, connects MongoDB, starts grammY polling, and starts alert polling.
src/bot.js creates the grammY bot and callback handlers.
src/commands contains Telegram slash commands.
src/services contains market data, watchlist, alert, user, and polling logic.
src/lib contains config, database, and logging helpers.
src/utils contains formatting and cache helpers.

Setup

1) Install Node.js 18 or newer.
2) Create a Telegram bot with BotFather.
3) Create a MongoDB database.
4) Copy .env.sample to .env.
5) Set TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and MONGODB_URI.
6) Optionally set COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY.
7) Run npm install.
8) Run npm run dev.

Commands

/start opens the main menu.
Example response: Welcome to Crypto Watcher with buttons for Price Lookup, Watchlist, Add Alert, and Help.

/help shows commands and examples.

/price BTC shows Bitcoin price and 24h change.

/addwatch ETH adds Ethereum to your watchlist.

/watchlist lists saved coins and prices.

/removewatch ETH removes Ethereum from your watchlist.

/alert BTC above 90000 creates a one-time alert.

/alert SOL below 100 creates a below alert.

/alerts lists your active and triggered alerts.

/removealert <id> removes an alert that belongs to you.

Integrations

CoinGecko endpoints used:
https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/search
https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/simple/price

CoinMarketCap endpoint used only when COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY is set:
https://pro-api.coinmarketcap.com/v2/cryptocurrency/quotes/latest

External API calls have timeouts, logs, and fallback behavior. If live APIs fail and cached data exists, stale data is shown clearly. If no usable data exists, the user receives a friendly API-down message.

Database

Collections:
users stores Telegram user profile and status.
coins stores cached coin metadata.
watchlist_items stores user-specific watchlist entries.
alerts stores active, triggered, and deleted alerts.
cached_prices stores last known market data.
notification_logs stores alert notification delivery attempts.

Indexes are created for application fields only. The code never creates an _id index.

Deployment

Use one Render web service or worker-style service that runs npm start. Set TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and MONGODB_URI. COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY is optional. The build command is npm run build and the start command is npm start.

Troubleshooting

If Telegram polling conflicts occur during deploy overlap, the runner logs the conflict, backs off, and retries.

If MongoDB fails, the bot exits with a clear message because persistent storage is required for alerts and watchlists.

If prices fail, check CoinGecko availability and rate limits. Add COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY for fallback coverage.

Logs are production-safe and only print env presence booleans, never secrets.

Bot: Production-ready Telegram crypto price and alerts bot

Summary:
A single-process Node.js ESM Telegram bot built with grammY that lets users manage crypto watchlists, look up live prices, create above and below price alerts, and receive notifications when targets are hit.

The bot uses a provider abstraction over CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap so price data can be fetched consistently, cached safely, and degraded gracefully when one provider is unavailable. MongoDB is used for durable user, watchlist, alert, and notification state, while in-memory caching protects external APIs from excessive calls and improves response speed.

The design prioritizes simple Telegram UX, reliable alert delivery, predictable error handling, and operational safety within the constraint of one Node.js service/process.

Product goals:
The bot should provide a fast and simple Telegram interface for everyday crypto tracking.

1) Users can look up a coin price with a command such as /price btc and receive current price, 24h percentage change, provider timestamp, and quick actions.

2) Users can build a personal watchlist by adding and removing coin symbols, then view the watchlist with current prices and 24h changes.

3) Users can create price alerts for specific coins using above or below conditions. Alerts should be easy to list, remove, pause, or recreate.

4) The bot should notify users when alert targets are reached and avoid repeated spam for the same trigger.

5) The bot should handle provider downtime, invalid symbols, rate limits, and slow responses gracefully. When live data is unavailable, it should use cached data where safe and clearly tell users when data may be stale.

6) The UX should use Telegram inline buttons for common actions such as add to watchlist, remove from watchlist, add alert, list alerts, and refresh price.

7) The system should be production-ready but intentionally simple: one Node.js process, grammY for Telegram, MongoDB for persistence, in-memory caches for runtime optimization, and no additional queues or infrastructure.

High-level architecture:
The bot runs as a single Node.js ESM service using grammY. It starts with TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN from environment variables, initializes MongoDB, loads bot commands, registers command and callback handlers, and starts an in-process alert scheduler.

Core components:

1) Telegram interface layer
Handles grammY commands, callback queries, message parsing, inline keyboards, and response formatting. This layer should stay thin and delegate business logic to services.

2) User service
Creates or updates user records when a user interacts with the bot. Stores Telegram user id, username, locale, preferences, and status.

3) Coin resolution service
Normalizes user input such as btc, BTC, bitcoin, eth, or ethereum into a canonical coin identity. This is important because symbols are ambiguous. The service should prefer known high-liquidity mappings and store provider-specific ids.

4) Price provider layer
Defines a common internal interface for fetching prices, 24h change, market metadata, and symbol search. Implement adapters for CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap. One provider can be primary and the other fallback. Responses should be normalized into one internal format.

5) Cache layer
Uses in-memory maps with TTLs for recent prices, coin search results, provider health, and negative lookups. This reduces API usage, improves latency, and protects the bot from rate limits. MongoDB can optionally store longer-lived coin metadata and last known prices, but hot cache should remain in memory.

6) Watchlist service
Manages user watchlist items in MongoDB. It validates coin symbols through the coin resolution service and avoids duplicates.

7) Alert service
Manages alert creation, listing, removal, state transitions, and trigger evaluation. Alerts are persisted in MongoDB so they survive process restarts.

8) Notification service
Sends Telegram messages when alerts trigger. It records notification attempts and results to support idempotency and debugging.

9) Alert scheduler
Runs inside the same Node.js process on a fixed interval. It loads active alerts, groups them by coin, fetches prices efficiently in batches when possible, evaluates thresholds, and dispatches notifications. It should use a simple in-process lock flag to prevent overlapping scheduler ticks.

10) Error handling and fallback layer
Centralizes user-safe errors. Provider errors should not leak raw stack traces. If live data fails but cached data exists, the bot should respond with a stale-data notice. If no data is available, it should show a clear API down message and suggest retrying later.

The recommended runtime flow is request driven for commands and interval driven for alert checks. Because the service is a single process, all background tasks must be lightweight, bounded, and defensive against slow APIs.

Data model:
Use MongoDB for durable persistence. In-memory maps are used for short-lived runtime caching only.

Suggested collections:

1) users
Fields: telegramUserId, chatId, username, firstName, languageCode, timezone, currencyPreference, isBlocked, createdAt, updatedAt, lastSeenAt.

Purpose: identify where to send notifications, store user preferences, and track whether messages can still be delivered.

2) coins
Fields: coinId, symbol, name, aliases, providerIds, rank, isActive, lastResolvedAt, createdAt, updatedAt.

Purpose: cache canonical coin metadata and reduce repeated provider search calls. providerIds can include the CoinGecko id and CoinMarketCap id when available.

3) watchlistItems
Fields: userId, coinId, symbol, name, createdAt.

Recommended indexes: unique combination of userId and coinId.

Purpose: store each user’s watchlist without duplicates.

4) alerts
Fields: userId, chatId, coinId, symbol, name, direction, targetPrice, currency, status, triggerOnce, cooldownMinutes, lastCheckedPrice, lastCheckedAt, triggeredAt, lastNotifiedAt, createdAt, updatedAt.

Valid direction values: above, below.

Valid status values: active, triggered, paused, deleted.

Purpose: store active and historical price alerts. For a simple UX, alerts should default to triggerOnce true, meaning they become triggered after notification. A future setting can support recurring alerts with cooldown.

5) notificationLogs
Fields: userId, chatId, alertId, coinId, type, message, status, telegramMessageId, errorCode, errorMessage, createdAt.

Purpose: record alert notification attempts and prevent duplicate sends during scheduler retries.

6) providerStatus
Fields: providerName, status, lastSuccessAt, lastFailureAt, failureCount, lastError, updatedAt.

Purpose: track provider health and support fallback decisions.

7) optional priceSnapshots
Fields: coinId, currency, price, change24h, providerName, fetchedAt, expiresAt.

Purpose: store last known prices across restarts if desired. This is optional because the main price cache can be in memory, but storing last known values improves API down fallback behavior after a restart.

In-memory caches:

1) priceCache keyed by coinId and currency, with a short TTL such as 30 to 60 seconds.

2) coinSearchCache keyed by normalized user input, with a longer TTL such as several hours.

3) negativeLookupCache keyed by invalid symbol input, with a shorter TTL such as 5 to 15 minutes.

4) providerHealthCache keyed by provider name, used to avoid hammering a failing API.

Data consistency principles:

1) Store canonical coin identity, not only raw symbols.

2) Keep alerts durable before confirming creation to the user.

3) Mark alerts as triggered before or atomically with notification logging where practical to reduce duplicate notifications.

4) Treat external prices as eventually consistent and always include timestamps when data may be cached or stale.

Key flows:
Onboarding flow:

1) User sends /start.

2) Bot creates or updates the user record.

3) Bot replies with a short explanation and inline buttons: Price lookup, Add to watchlist, My watchlist, Create alert, My alerts.

Price lookup flow:

1) User sends /price btc.

2) Bot normalizes btc and resolves it to a canonical coin.

3) Bot checks the in-memory price cache.

4) If cache is fresh, return the cached price immediately.

5) If cache is missing or expired, fetch from the primary provider.

6) If the primary provider fails, fetch from the fallback provider.

7) If both fail but a last known price exists, reply with stale price plus an API down notice.

8) If no usable data exists, reply with a graceful fallback message.

9) Response includes inline buttons such as Add to watchlist, Add alert, Refresh, and View watchlist.

Watchlist add flow:

1) User sends /add btc or taps Add to watchlist from a price result.

2) Bot resolves the coin.

3) Bot creates the watchlist item if it does not already exist.

4) Bot confirms and offers buttons for View watchlist and Add alert.

Watchlist list flow:

1) User sends /watchlist.

2) Bot loads the user’s watchlist.

3) Bot groups coin ids and fetches prices efficiently, using cache where possible.

4) Bot returns a compact list with price and 24h change.

5) Each row or summary includes quick actions where practical: Refresh, Remove, Add alert.

Watchlist remove flow:

1) User sends /remove btc or taps Remove.

2) Bot resolves or matches the coin from the user’s watchlist.

3) Bot deletes the item and confirms.

Alert creation flow:

1) User sends a command such as /alert btc above 70000 or taps Add alert.

2) Bot validates symbol, direction, and target price.

3) Bot fetches current price to provide context.

4) Bot stores an active alert in MongoDB.

5) Bot confirms with current price, target price, direction, and buttons for My alerts and Remove alert.

Alert listing flow:

1) User sends /alerts.

2) Bot lists active alerts first, then recently triggered alerts if useful.

3) Each alert shows coin, direction, target, current or last checked price, and status.

4) Inline buttons allow removing or pausing individual alerts.

Alert removal flow:

1) User sends /removealert alertId or taps a Remove alert button.

2) Bot verifies that the alert belongs to the user.

3) Bot marks the alert deleted rather than hard deleting it.

4) Bot confirms removal.

Notification flow:

1) Scheduler wakes up at a fixed interval such as every 30 to 60 seconds.

2) Scheduler loads active alerts due for checking.

3) Scheduler groups alerts by coin and currency.

4) Scheduler fetches current prices with cache and provider fallback.

5) For each alert, scheduler checks whether the condition is met: above means current price is greater than or equal to target; below means current price is less than or equal to target.

6) If met, scheduler marks trigger state and sends a Telegram notification.

7) Notification includes coin, current price, target price, direction, 24h change, and buttons such as View alerts, Create another alert, and View price.

8) If Telegram reports that the user blocked the bot, mark the user as blocked and stop sending future notifications.

Provider failure flow:

1) On timeout, rate limit, invalid response, or server error, record provider failure.

2) Try fallback provider if available and healthy.

3) If all providers fail, use fresh-enough cached data if available.

4) If only stale data is available, clearly label it as last known price.

1) Callback payloads should be compact and contain action plus stable ids, not untrusted full user input.

2) Every callback must verify ownership when modifying user data.

planSections.productGoals:
The bot should provide a fast and simple Telegram interface for everyday crypto tracking.

1) Users can look up a coin price with a command such as /price btc and receive current price, 24h percentage change, provider timestamp, and quick actions.

2) Users can build a personal watchlist by adding and removing coin symbols, then view the watchlist with current prices and 24h changes.

3) Users can create price alerts for specific coins using above or below conditions. Alerts should be easy to list, remove, pause, or recreate.

4) The bot should notify users when alert targets are reached and avoid repeated spam for the same trigger.

5) The bot should handle provider downtime, invalid symbols, rate limits, and slow responses gracefully. When live data is unavailable, it should use cached data where safe and clearly tell users when data may be stale.

6) The UX should use Telegram inline buttons for common actions such as add to watchlist, remove from watchlist, add alert, list alerts, and refresh price.

7) The system should be production-ready but intentionally simple: one Node.js process, grammY for Telegram, MongoDB for persistence, in-memory caches for runtime optimization, and no additional queues or infrastructure.
planSections.highLevelArchitecture:
The bot runs as a single Node.js ESM service using grammY. It starts with TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN from environment variables, initializes MongoDB, loads bot commands, registers command and callback handlers, and starts an in-process alert scheduler.

Core components:

1) Telegram interface layer
Handles grammY commands, callback queries, message parsing, inline keyboards, and response formatting. This layer should stay thin and delegate business logic to services.

2) User service
Creates or updates user records when a user interacts with the bot. Stores Telegram user id, username, locale, preferences, and status.

3) Coin resolution service
Normalizes user input such as btc, BTC, bitcoin, eth, or ethereum into a canonical coin identity. This is important because symbols are ambiguous. The service should prefer known high-liquidity mappings and store provider-specific ids.

4) Price provider layer
Defines a common internal interface for fetching prices, 24h change, market metadata, and symbol search. Implement adapters for CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap. One provider can be primary and the other fallback. Responses should be normalized into one internal format.

5) Cache layer
Uses in-memory maps with TTLs for recent prices, coin search results, provider health, and negative lookups. This reduces API usage, improves latency, and protects the bot from rate limits. MongoDB can optionally store longer-lived coin metadata and last known prices, but hot cache should remain in memory.

6) Watchlist service
Manages user watchlist items in MongoDB. It validates coin symbols through the coin resolution service and avoids duplicates.

7) Alert service
Manages alert creation, listing, removal, state transitions, and trigger evaluation. Alerts are persisted in MongoDB so they survive process restarts.

8) Notification service
Sends Telegram messages when alerts trigger. It records notification attempts and results to support idempotency and debugging.

9) Alert scheduler
Runs inside the same Node.js process on a fixed interval. It loads active alerts, groups them by coin, fetches prices efficiently in batches when possible, evaluates thresholds, and dispatches notifications. It should use a simple in-process lock flag to prevent overlapping scheduler ticks.

10) Error handling and fallback layer
Centralizes user-safe errors. Provider errors should not leak raw stack traces. If live data fails but cached data exists, the bot should respond with a stale-data notice. If no data is available, it should show a clear API down message and suggest retrying later.

The recommended runtime flow is request driven for commands and interval driven for alert checks. Because the service is a single process, all background tasks must be lightweight, bounded, and defensive against slow APIs.
planSections.dataModel:
Use MongoDB for durable persistence. In-memory maps are used for short-lived runtime caching only.

Suggested collections:

1) users
Fields: telegramUserId, chatId, username, firstName, languageCode, timezone, currencyPreference, isBlocked, createdAt, updatedAt, lastSeenAt.

Purpose: identify where to send notifications, store user preferences, and track whether messages can still be delivered.

2) coins
Fields: coinId, symbol, name, aliases, providerIds, rank, isActive, lastResolvedAt, createdAt, updatedAt.

Purpose: cache canonical coin metadata and reduce repeated provider search calls. providerIds can include the CoinGecko id and CoinMarketCap id when available.

3) watchlistItems
Fields: userId, coinId, symbol, name, createdAt.

Recommended indexes: unique combination of userId and coinId.

Purpose: store each user’s watchlist without duplicates.

4) alerts
Fields: userId, chatId, coinId, symbol, name, direction, targetPrice, currency, status, triggerOnce, cooldownMinutes, lastCheckedPrice, lastCheckedAt, triggeredAt, lastNotifiedAt, createdAt, updatedAt.

Valid direction values: above, below.

Valid status values: active, triggered, paused, deleted.

Purpose: store active and historical price alerts. For a simple UX, alerts should default to triggerOnce true, meaning they become triggered after notification. A future setting can support recurring alerts with cooldown.

5) notificationLogs
Fields: userId, chatId, alertId, coinId, type, message, status, telegramMessageId, errorCode, errorMessage, createdAt.

Purpose: record alert notification attempts and prevent duplicate sends during scheduler retries.

6) providerStatus
Fields: providerName, status, lastSuccessAt, lastFailureAt, failureCount, lastError, updatedAt.

Purpose: track provider health and support fallback decisions.

7) optional priceSnapshots
Fields: coinId, currency, price, change24h, providerName, fetchedAt, expiresAt.

Purpose: store last known prices across restarts if desired. This is optional because the main price cache can be in memory, but storing last known values improves API down fallback behavior after a restart.

In-memory caches:

1) priceCache keyed by coinId and currency, with a short TTL such as 30 to 60 seconds.

2) coinSearchCache keyed by normalized user input, with a longer TTL such as several hours.

3) negativeLookupCache keyed by invalid symbol input, with a shorter TTL such as 5 to 15 minutes.

4) providerHealthCache keyed by provider name, used to avoid hammering a failing API.

Data consistency principles:

1) Store canonical coin identity, not only raw symbols.

2) Keep alerts durable before confirming creation to the user.

3) Mark alerts as triggered before or atomically with notification logging where practical to reduce duplicate notifications.

4) Treat external prices as eventually consistent and always include timestamps when data may be cached or stale.
planSections.keyFlows:
Onboarding flow:

1) User sends /start.

2) Bot creates or updates the user record.

3) Bot replies with a short explanation and inline buttons: Price lookup, Add to watchlist, My watchlist, Create alert, My alerts.

Price lookup flow:

1) User sends /price btc.

2) Bot normalizes btc and resolves it to a canonical coin.

3) Bot checks the in-memory price cache.

4) If cache is fresh, return the cached price immediately.

5) If cache is missing or expired, fetch from the primary provider.

6) If the primary provider fails, fetch from the fallback provider.

7) If both fail but a last known price exists, reply with stale price plus an API down notice.

8) If no usable data exists, reply with a graceful fallback message.

9) Response includes inline buttons such as Add to watchlist, Add alert, Refresh, and View watchlist.

Watchlist add flow:

1) User sends /add btc or taps Add to watchlist from a price result.

2) Bot resolves the coin.

3) Bot creates the watchlist item if it does not already exist.

4) Bot confirms and offers buttons for View watchlist and Add alert.

Watchlist list flow:

1) User sends /watchlist.

2) Bot loads the user’s watchlist.

3) Bot groups coin ids and fetches prices efficiently, using cache where possible.

4) Bot returns a compact list with price and 24h change.

5) Each row or summary includes quick actions where practical: Refresh, Remove, Add alert.

Watchlist remove flow:

1) User sends /remove btc or taps Remove.

2) Bot resolves or matches the coin from the user’s watchlist.

3) Bot deletes the item and confirms.

Alert creation flow:

1) User sends a command such as /alert btc above 70000 or taps Add alert.

2) Bot validates symbol, direction, and target price.

3) Bot fetches current price to provide context.

4) Bot stores an active alert in MongoDB.

5) Bot confirms with current price, target price, direction, and buttons for My alerts and Remove alert.

Alert listing flow:

1) User sends /alerts.

2) Bot lists active alerts first, then recently triggered alerts if useful.

3) Each alert shows coin, direction, target, current or last checked price, and status.

4) Inline buttons allow removing or pausing individual alerts.

Alert removal flow:

1) User sends /removealert alertId or taps a Remove alert button.

2) Bot verifies that the alert belongs to the user.

3) Bot marks the alert deleted rather than hard deleting it.

4) Bot confirms removal.

Notification flow:

1) Scheduler wakes up at a fixed interval such as every 30 to 60 seconds.

2) Scheduler loads active alerts due for checking.

3) Scheduler groups alerts by coin and currency.

4) Scheduler fetches current prices with cache and provider fallback.

5) For each alert, scheduler checks whether the condition is met: above means current price is greater than or equal to target; below means current price is less than or equal to target.

6) If met, scheduler marks trigger state and sends a Telegram notification.

7) Notification includes coin, current price, target price, direction, 24h change, and buttons such as View alerts, Create another alert, and View price.

8) If Telegram reports that the user blocked the bot, mark the user as blocked and stop sending future notifications.

Provider failure flow:

1) On timeout, rate limit, invalid response, or server error, record provider failure.

2) Try fallback provider if available and healthy.

3) If all providers fail, use fresh-enough cached data if available.

4) If only stale data is available, clearly label it as last known price.

5) If no data is available, show: Price API is temporarily unavailable. Please try again later.

Inline button flow:

1) Callback payloads should be compact and contain action plus stable ids, not untrusted full user input.

2) Every callback must verify ownership when modifying user data.

3) Callback handlers should answer callback queries quickly to avoid Telegram loading spinners.

4) For destructive actions, either confirm with a second button or make removal easy to undo where appropriate.

DOCS.md.content:
Crypto Watcher Bot

Crypto Watcher is a Telegram bot for cryptocurrency prices, watchlists, and price alerts. It uses CoinGecko first, then CoinMarketCap only when COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY is configured. MongoDB stores users, watchlists, alerts, coin metadata, and cached prices.

Commands

/start
Shows the welcome message and inline buttons for Price Lookup, Watchlist, Add Alert, and Help.

/help
Lists commands and examples.

/price <symbol>
Shows current USD price and 24h change.
Example: /price BTC

/watchlist
Shows your saved coins with prices when available.

/addwatch <symbol>
Adds a coin to your watchlist.
Example: /addwatch SOL

/removewatch <symbol>
Removes a coin from your watchlist.
Example: /removewatch ETH

/alert <symbol> <above|below> <price>
Creates a one-time alert.
Examples: /alert BTC above 90000, /alert ETH below 2500

/alerts
Lists your active and recently triggered alerts with IDs.

/removealert <id>
Removes an alert. Use /alerts to find the ID.

Environment variables

TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN is required. It is the Telegram token from BotFather.

MONGODB_URI is required. It stores users, watchlists, alerts, cached coin metadata, cached prices, and notification logs.

COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY is optional. If present, CoinMarketCap is used as a fallback when CoinGecko is unavailable.

ALERT_POLL_MS is optional and defaults to 60000.

MARKET_TIMEOUT_MS is optional and defaults to 10000.

PRICE_CACHE_TTL_MS is optional and defaults to 45000.

SYMBOL_CACHE_TTL_MS is optional and defaults to 21600000.

Setup

1) Copy .env.sample to .env.
2) Set TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and MONGODB_URI.
3) Run npm install.
4) Run npm run dev for local development.
5) Run npm start for production.

Deployment notes

The bot runs as one Node.js process. It uses grammY long polling through @grammyjs/runner. On boot it clears any Telegram webhook with drop_pending_updates to avoid webhook and polling conflicts.

Alert notifications

The in-process polling loop checks active alerts at ALERT_POLL_MS. It groups alerts by coin, fetches prices in batches where possible, marks triggered alerts inactive, and sends one notification per triggered alert.

Troubleshooting

If the bot exits on startup, verify TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and MONGODB_URI are set.

If prices are unavailable, CoinGecko may be rate limited or down. If cached prices exist, the bot labels them as cached or stale. If no cache exists, it asks the user to try later.

If MongoDB fails to connect, check the network allowlist, username, password, and database URI.

Logs never print secrets. Startup logs show only whether each env var is set.

README.md.content:
Crypto Watcher Bot

A production-ready Telegram bot for crypto prices, watchlists, and one-time price alerts.

Features

1) /price BTC returns USD price and 24h change.
2) /watchlist, /addwatch, and /removewatch manage saved coins.
3) /alert, /alerts, and /removealert manage above and below alerts.
4) Inline buttons support refresh, watchlist, add alert, remove, and help actions.
5) CoinGecko is the primary market API.
6) CoinMarketCap is an optional fallback when COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY is present.
7) MongoDB stores users, watchlists, alerts, cached coin metadata, cached prices, and notification logs.
8) The alert polling loop runs in the same Node.js process.

Architecture

src/index.js boots the process, validates env vars, connects MongoDB, starts grammY polling, and starts alert polling.
src/bot.js creates the grammY bot and callback handlers.
src/commands contains Telegram slash commands.
src/services contains market data, watchlist, alert, user, and polling logic.
src/lib contains config, database, and logging helpers.
src/utils contains formatting and cache helpers.

Setup

1) Install Node.js 18 or newer.
2) Create a Telegram bot with BotFather.
3) Create a MongoDB database.
4) Copy .env.sample to .env.
5) Set TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and MONGODB_URI.
6) Optionally set COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY.
7) Run npm install.
8) Run npm run dev.

Commands

/start opens the main menu.
Example response: Welcome to Crypto Watcher with buttons for Price Lookup, Watchlist, Add Alert, and Help.

/help shows commands and examples.

/price BTC shows Bitcoin price and 24h change.

/addwatch ETH adds Ethereum to your watchlist.

/watchlist lists saved coins and prices.

/removewatch ETH removes Ethereum from your watchlist.

/alert BTC above 90000 creates a one-time alert.

/alert SOL below 100 creates a below alert.

/alerts lists your active and triggered alerts.

/removealert <id> removes an alert that belongs to you.

Integrations

CoinGecko endpoints used:
https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/search
https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/simple/price

CoinMarketCap endpoint used only when COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY is set:
https://pro-api.coinmarketcap.com/v2/cryptocurrency/quotes/latest

External API calls have timeouts, logs, and fallback behavior. If live APIs fail and cached data exists, stale data is shown clearly. If no usable data exists, the user receives a friendly API-down message.

Database

Collections:
users stores Telegram user profile and status.
coins stores cached coin metadata.
watchlist_items stores user-specific watchlist entries.
alerts stores active, triggered, and deleted alerts.
cached_prices stores last known market data.
notification_logs stores alert notification delivery attempts.

Indexes are created for application fields only. The code never creates an _id index.

Deployment

Use one Render web service or worker-style service that runs npm start. Set TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and MONGODB_URI. COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY is optional. The build command is npm run build and the start command is npm start.

Troubleshooting

If Telegram polling conflicts occur during deploy overlap, the runner logs the conflict, backs off, and retries.

If MongoDB fails, the bot exits with a clear message because persistent storage is required for alerts and watchlists.

If prices fail, check CoinGecko availability and rate limits. Add COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY for fallback coverage.

Logs are production-safe and only print env presence booleans, never secrets.

The bot should provide a fast and simple Telegram interface for everyday crypto tracking.
